characters: Kofi: an eight-year-old Ghanaian boy in Primary 3, short cropped black hair, wearing a bright yellow polo shirt and blue shorts.
Ama: Kofi’s ten-year-old sister, neat braided hair with red beads, wearing a green dress.
Yaw: Kofi’s nine-year-old cousin, wearing a striped orange-and-white t-shirt and khaki shorts.
Maame: Kofi and Ama’s mother, a kind seamstress and stationer in her thirties, wearing a blue-and-gold wax-print dress.

narrationPlan.voice: Warm, lively Ghanaian storyteller (en-GH); bright and clear on all coin counts.
narrationPlan.pace: Medium-slow (about 105 words per minute) so Primary 2–3 listeners can follow the arithmetic easily.
notes: Emphasise the difference between revenue (ten cedis) and profit (five cedis) on page 8.

music: Optional cheerful acoustic highlife guitar pluck; off by default.
culturalNotes: Uses Ghana cedis and pesewas accurately (100 pesewas = 1 cedi; 5 cedis ÷ 10 items = 50 pesewas per item).
reviewQuestions: Is the arithmetic (1 + 2 + 2 = 5 cedis capital; 10 × 1 = 10 cedis revenue; 10 − 5 = 5 cedis profit) crystal clear for Primary 2–3?

pages.brief: Sunny Ghanaian family veranda: Kofi (8, yellow polo shirt, blue shorts) holding up one shiny coin while Maame (blue-and-gold wax-print dress) smiles beside a table with colourful card offcuts and sewing tools.
pages.narration: Cheerful, eager voice for Kofi; warm, practical guidance from Maame.

pages.brief: Shaded courtyard reading club: Ghanaian children reading storybooks at a wooden table; Kofi and Ama (10, braided hair with red beads, green dress) pointing thoughtfully at a book where a child is trying to find their page.
pages.narration: Curious observation leading to Ama’s bright idea.

pages.brief: Friendly neighbourhood stationery counter: Kofi looking down at one coin in his palm while Ama and cousin Yaw (9, striped orange-and-white t-shirt) look at colourful manila card sheets and a glue bottle on the counter (no text or price tags).
pages.narration: Honest realisation on "You cannot start most businesses with just one cedi alone".

pages.brief: Close view around a wooden table: Kofi, Ama and Yaw smiling as they bring their coins together into a neat row of five coins beside the coloured card sheets and glue.
pages.narration: Upbeat teamwork on the addition: "One cedi plus two cedis plus two cedis equalled five cedis".

pages.brief: Sunny veranda table: Yaw folding card triangles with a wooden ruler, Ama trimming with safety scissors, and Kofi drawing cute animal faces (a tortoise, a goat, a bird, no letters) on ten bright corner bookmarks.
pages.narration: Rhythmic, industrious energy as the three children work together.

pages.brief: Kofi demonstrating how a colourful tortoise corner bookmark slips snugly onto the top corner of an open picture book, while Ama and Yaw line up the remaining nine bookmarks on a clean cloth.
pages.narration: Clear, step-by-step explanation of cost per unit (50 pesewas) and fair selling price (1 cedi).

pages.brief: Courtyard reading club table: smiling children holding books with colourful corner bookmarks attached, while Kofi, Ama and Yaw count ten shiny coins in a small wooden bowl.
Around the veranda table: Maame pointing gently as Kofi, Ama and Yaw divide the ten coins into two neat groups of five coins on a woven mat.
pages.narration: Crucial numeracy moment: 10 cedis revenue minus 5 cedis cost equals 5 cedis profit.

pages.brief: Warm golden-hour scene on the veranda: Kofi, Ama and Yaw smiling proudly together with their cloth coin pouch and a fresh pack of coloured card, with Maame clapping behind them.
pages.narration: Warm, proud finish celebrating honesty, teamwork and smart arithmetic.

teacherGuide.overview: An engaging Primary 2–3 enterprise and numeracy story that demystifies how a small business works: identifying a customer problem, realising that 1 cedi alone cannot buy 5 cedis of materials, pooling startup capital (1 + 2 + 2 = 5 cedis), pricing fairly (1 cedi per bookmark), and distinguishing total revenue (10 cedis) from profit (10 − 5 = 5 cedis).
learningGoals: Explain why businesses exist to solve real problems for customers.
Add startup capital contributions (1 + 2 + 2 = 5 cedis) and calculate unit cost (5 cedis ÷ 10 bookmarks = 50 pesewas each).
Distinguish between total sales (revenue = 10 cedis) and actual gain (profit = 10 − 5 = 5 cedis).
Practise fair teamwork and honest record-keeping.

beforeReading: Preview the title and cover illustration with learners and ask what real-world problem or question the characters might face.
whileReading: Pause at the embedded comprehension and vocabulary activities to check understanding and discuss the evidence in the text.
afterReading: Fold-a-Corner Bookmark Craft: Using scrap paper squares, fold triangular corner bookmarks in class and test them on a reader.
Shopkeeper Maths Role-Play: Act out buying materials for 5 cedis, selling 10 items at 1 cedi each, separating the 10 coins into 5 cedis (cost recovery) and 5 cedis (profit).
discussion: Why could Kofi not buy the manila card and glue with only his single one-cedi coin?
What problem at the reading club made people happy to pay 1 cedi for a corner bookmark?
Why did Maame remind Yaw that having 10 cedis in the bowl did not mean they had made 10 cedis of profit?
Why did the partners put 5 cedis back into their capital pouch before sharing the profit?
reflection: Why did the partners put 5 cedis back into their capital pouch before sharing the profit?

investigation.title: Revenue vs Profit Coin Sorting
materials: Ten paper circles or bottle tops labelled "1 cedi" and two small bowls labelled "Cost of Materials (5 cedis)" and "Profit".
steps: Place all 10 bottle-top "cedis" on the desk to represent the 10 cedis of revenue from selling 10 bookmarks.
Count out 5 bottle tops and place them into the "Cost of Materials" bowl to pay back what the card and glue cost.
Count the remaining bottle tops and place them into the "Profit" bowl (10 − 5 = 5 cedis).

reviewerNotes: Confirm the vowel in the first syllable (oh vs aw).
Confirm vowel quality and whether the final syllable is stressed.
